quests.hint: Use 'Would it be possible to…?' for a very polite, formal request in service contexts.
quests.explanation: 'Would it be possible to have a room on a higher floor?' is more formal than 'Can I have.' This structure is perfect for hotels, offices, or any situation where extra politeness is expected or appreciated.
quests.situationText: You are checking into a hotel and would like to politely request a room with a nicer view.
quests.sampleAnswer: Good evening! Would it be possible to have a room on a higher floor with a view? I'd be very grateful if so.
quests.correctAnswer: room on a higher floor with a view
acceptedSynonyms: room on a higher floor with a view
a room with a view if possible

quests.hint: Use 'Would you mind not…?' to ask someone to stop doing something disruptive, very politely.
quests.explanation: 'Would you mind not smoking?' is far gentler than 'Stop smoking!' The modal 'would' combined with 'not' makes this one of the most politely phrased requests in the English language.
quests.situationText: You are in a café and the person beside you has started smoking near the non-smoking section.
quests.sampleAnswer: Excuse me, would you mind not smoking here? I'm quite sensitive to it. I believe there's a smoking area just outside?
quests.correctAnswer: would you mind not smoking here
acceptedSynonyms: would you mind not smoking here

quests.hint: Use 'Do you think I could possibly…?' for the most indirect and considerate form of a request.
quests.explanation: Adding 'possibly' creates the most tentative and considerate form of a request in English. It signals maximum respect for the other person's wishes and comfort, which is especially important in tight or shared spaces.
quests.situationText: You are on a full flight and want to ask the passenger beside you if you could swap seats.
quests.sampleAnswer: Do you think I could possibly swap seats with you? I'm feeling a little unwell sitting by the window. I'd really appreciate it.
quests.correctAnswer: swap seats with you

quests.hint: Start a phone booking with 'I'd like to make an appointment for… Is [time/date] available?'
quests.explanation: 'I'd like to make an appointment' is the standard opening phrase for booking by phone. Following with your preferred time shows initiative and makes the booking process more efficient for both parties.
quests.situationText: You call the dentist's surgery to book a routine check-up for some time next week.
quests.sampleAnswer: Hi, I'd like to make an appointment for a routine check-up, please. Is next Tuesday morning available at all?
quests.correctAnswer: routine dental check-up

quests.hint: When confirming an appointment, repeat the key details back: date, time, and location.
quests.explanation: Repeating appointment details back confirms accuracy and prevents missed meetings. 'So that's Thursday at three at the city centre branch?' ensures both parties have identical information.
quests.situationText: The receptionist has given you an appointment time and you want to confirm all the details.
quests.sampleAnswer: So that's Wednesday at two thirty at the main clinic on Park Road? Perfect - I'll be there. Thank you so much!
quests.correctAnswer: Wednesday at two thirty is perfect
acceptedSynonyms: Wednesday at two thirty is perfect

quests.hint: Cancel an appointment with 'I'm calling to cancel my appointment on… I'm so sorry for the short notice.'
quests.explanation: Apologizing for short notice when canceling shows consideration. Offering to reschedule ('Could we rearrange?') shows you still value the appointment and are not simply canceling without regard.
quests.situationText: Something urgent has come up and you need to cancel your doctor's appointment for tomorrow morning.
quests.sampleAnswer: Hi, I'm calling to cancel my ten o'clock appointment tomorrow morning. I'm so sorry for the short notice - could we possibly rearrange for later in the week?
quests.correctAnswer: calling to cancel my appointment

quests.hint: When interrupting, say 'I'm so sorry to interrupt, but…' to show respect for the ongoing conversation.
quests.explanation: 'I'm sorry to interrupt' is the polite English formula for cutting in. Without this opener, interrupting sounds rude and abrupt. With it, you signal consideration for the person you are interrupting.
quests.situationText: Your colleague is on an important call and you need to ask them something urgent right now.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm so sorry to interrupt - could I just steal one second of your time? I need a quick word about tomorrow's client meeting.
quests.correctAnswer: steal one second of your time
acceptedSynonyms: steal one second of your time

quests.hint: Apologize for a work mistake: 'I owe you an apology for… It won't happen again.'
quests.explanation: 'I owe you an apology' is a strong, accountable professional phrase. Promising 'it won't happen again' shows you take responsibility and are committed to improvement - both highly valued in workplace culture.
quests.situationText: You sent the wrong version of a file to an important client and your manager needs to hear about it.
quests.sampleAnswer: I owe you a genuine apology for sending the wrong file to the client. It was completely my error and I assure you it won't happen again.
quests.correctAnswer: I owe you a genuine apology
acceptedSynonyms: I owe you a genuine apology

quests.hint: Clarify a misunderstanding: 'I think there may have been a misunderstanding. What I meant was…'
quests.explanation: 'There may have been a misunderstanding' is non-accusatory and professional. 'What I meant was' explains your original intention clearly without blaming the other person for misinterpreting what you said.
quests.situationText: A colleague seems upset about something you said in a meeting that was clearly misinterpreted.
quests.sampleAnswer: I think there may have been a misunderstanding - what I meant was that the timeline needs more flexibility, not that the team was moving too slowly. I'm sorry if it came across that way.
quests.correctAnswer: there may have been a misunderstanding
acceptedSynonyms: there may have been a misunderstanding

quests.hint: Express excitement with 'I can't wait for…' - it sounds natural and genuinely enthusiastic.
quests.explanation: 'I can't wait for the concert' is one of the most natural ways to express excited anticipation in English. It conveys positive impatience and genuine enthusiasm far more vividly than 'I'm excited about.'
quests.situationText: You just got tickets to see your absolute favourite band and you are telling your best friend.
quests.sampleAnswer: I literally can't wait for the concert next month! I've been a fan for over a decade - this is going to be extraordinary!
quests.correctAnswer: literally cannot wait for this concert
acceptedSynonyms: literally cannot wait for this concert

quests.hint: Show disappointment: 'I was really hoping that…' - it expresses the gap between expectation and reality.
quests.explanation: 'I was really hoping I'd get the job' expresses disappointment through contrast between what you wanted and what happened. It is more nuanced and relatable than the flat statement 'I'm disappointed.'
quests.situationText: You find out you didn't get the job you really wanted and tell your friend honestly about it.
quests.sampleAnswer: I was really hoping I'd get it - I genuinely thought the interview went well. Oh well, something better will come along. I have to believe that!
quests.correctAnswer: something better will come along

quests.hint: Describe nervousness with 'I have butterflies in my stomach' or 'I'm a bundle of nerves.'
quests.explanation: 'Butterflies in my stomach' is one of the most widely known English idioms for nervousness. 'I'm a bundle of nerves' is equally common. Both are vivid and expressive in a way that 'I'm nervous' simply is not.
quests.situationText: Tomorrow is your very important job interview and your friend asks how you are feeling tonight.
quests.sampleAnswer: Honestly, I'm a complete bundle of nerves! I already have butterflies and the interview isn't until tomorrow morning. Wish me luck, please!
quests.correctAnswer: complete bundle of nerves

quests.hint: Compliment cooking with 'This is absolutely delicious! You must give me the recipe.'
quests.explanation: 'This is absolutely delicious' is a strong, natural food compliment. Asking for the recipe signals you genuinely want to recreate the experience - which is the highest possible culinary praise you can give.
quests.situationText: A friend has cooked a three-course dinner especially for you and it is the best meal you have had in months.
quests.sampleAnswer: This is absolutely incredible! I have genuinely never tasted risotto this good. You must give me the recipe - please!
quests.correctAnswer: absolutely incredible

quests.hint: Compliment a presentation: 'That was really impressive - especially the part about…'
quests.explanation: Adding 'especially the part about…' makes a compliment specific and proves you were genuinely engaged. Vague compliments like 'nice presentation' feel hollow compared to specific ones that reference actual content.
quests.situationText: Your colleague has just delivered an excellent presentation to the whole department.
quests.sampleAnswer: That was genuinely really impressive! Especially the part about the Q3 data - you made a complex picture very clear and easy to follow. Well done!
quests.correctAnswer: genuinely really impressive work

quests.hint: Compliment someone's English: 'Your English is amazing! Did you study it for a long time?'
quests.explanation: Complimenting someone's language skills encourages and builds confidence. Following with a genuine question ('Did you study for a long time?') shows curiosity and invites them to share their journey.
quests.situationText: A new student in your English class speaks very fluently and you are genuinely impressed.
quests.sampleAnswer: Your English is honestly amazing! You sound so natural and confident. Did you study it for many years or did you learn it from living somewhere?
quests.correctAnswer: honestly amazing how confident you sound
acceptedSynonyms: honestly amazing how confident you sound

quests.hint: Respond to a compliment modestly: 'That's so kind of you to say! I was quite nervous, actually.'
quests.explanation: A modest English response to a compliment ('That's so kind of you to say') acknowledges it warmly without sounding arrogant. Adding honesty ('I was nervous') makes the response relatable and humanising.
quests.situationText: Someone tells you your presentation at the conference was the best one they heard all day.
quests.sampleAnswer: That's so incredibly kind of you to say! I was actually quite nervous beforehand, so I'm really glad it came across as well as that. Thank you!
quests.correctAnswer: incredibly kind of you to say that
acceptedSynonyms: incredibly kind of you to say that

quests.hint: Accept a compliment on your appearance: 'Thank you! I got it from…' to keep the conversation going.
quests.explanation: Saying where you got something in response to a compliment is a natural conversation extender. It transforms a simple thank-you into a genuine connection point and topic of shared interest.
quests.situationText: A colleague compliments the new jacket you are wearing and says it looks very stylish.
quests.sampleAnswer: Oh, thank you! I got it from a little vintage shop on the high street - it was an absolute bargain. I'm so pleased I found it!
quests.correctAnswer: absolute bargain from a vintage shop
acceptedSynonyms: absolute bargain from a vintage shop
found it at a vintage shop

quests.hint: Return a compliment: 'That's really sweet of you! I could say exactly the same about you!'
quests.explanation: 'I could say the same about you!' returns a compliment warmly and naturally. It validates what the person said while reflecting the positive feeling back toward them, creating a mutually uplifting exchange.
quests.situationText: Your friend compliments you on how organized and on top of things you always seem to be.
quests.sampleAnswer: That's really sweet of you! But honestly, I could say the exact same about you - you are one of the most focused and dedicated people I know. It's true!
quests.correctAnswer: say the exact same thing about you
acceptedSynonyms: say the exact same thing about you

quests.hint: Use 'Why don't we…?' for casual suggestions - it's collaborative and friendly.
quests.explanation: 'Why don't we try that new café?' is a collaborative suggestion that invites rather than commands. It makes the other person feel involved in the decision rather than being told what to do.
quests.situationText: Your friend seems bored on a Saturday afternoon and you want to suggest something fun.
quests.sampleAnswer: Why don't we check out that new street food market I read about? I heard it has food from about twenty different countries - sounds brilliant!
quests.correctAnswer: new street food market you should check out
acceptedSynonyms: new street food market you should check out

quests.hint: Suggest a solution with 'Have you thought about…?' to respect the person's autonomy.
quests.explanation: 'Have you thought about calling them directly?' is an indirect, respectful suggestion. A question rather than a command gives the person the choice to accept or dismiss your idea without feeling pressured.
quests.situationText: Your friend is stressed about a work conflict with a colleague and is not sure what to do.
quests.sampleAnswer: Have you thought about having a direct, calm conversation with them? It might feel scary, but it could clear the whole thing up in five minutes.
quests.correctAnswer: direct calm conversation
acceptedSynonyms: have you thought about talking to them

quests.hint: Give advice with 'If I were you, I'd…' to make your suggestion feel empathetic and considered.
quests.explanation: 'If I were you, I'd' uses the second conditional to express personal advice. It signals you are putting yourself in their position, which makes the advice feel considerate rather than judgmental or preachy.
quests.situationText: Your friend cannot decide whether to take a lower-paid job they are passionate about or stay safe.
quests.sampleAnswer: If I were you, I'd take the new job. You can always earn more money later, but you can't always find work that genuinely excites you like this.
quests.correctAnswer: if I were you I would take the new job
acceptedSynonyms: if I were you I would take the new job
you can earn more money later

quests.hint: Ask for advice: 'I'm not sure what to do about… Do you have any thoughts on it?'
quests.explanation: 'I'm not sure what to do' signals you are genuinely seeking guidance. 'Do you have any thoughts?' is an open invitation that makes the other person feel their perspective is valued and welcome.
quests.situationText: You are torn about whether to move cities for an exciting but risky job opportunity.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm genuinely not sure what to do about this job offer. It's an incredible opportunity but I'd have to relocate completely. Do you have any thoughts?
quests.correctAnswer: not sure what to do
acceptedSynonyms: would have to leave everyone I know

quests.hint: Give advice confidently: 'I'd strongly recommend… - it really worked for me personally.'
quests.explanation: 'I'd strongly recommend' conveys confidence without being pushy. Adding 'it really worked for me' makes the advice personal and credible - you are not just guessing, you are sharing direct experience.
quests.situationText: Your friend feels overwhelmed by their workload and asks how you manage yours so effectively.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'd strongly recommend the Pomodoro method - twenty-five minutes focused work, then a five-minute break. It really changed how productive I feel every single day.
quests.correctAnswer: Pomodoro method

quests.hint: Accept advice genuinely: 'That's really helpful - I hadn't thought of it that way at all.'
quests.explanation: Acknowledging that advice gave you a fresh perspective ('I hadn't thought of it that way') is a mature and encouraging response. It validates the person who gave the advice and shows genuine open-mindedness.
quests.situationText: A mentor has just given you thoughtful advice about how to handle a difficult work situation.
quests.sampleAnswer: That's actually really helpful, thank you. I hadn't thought of approaching it from that angle at all. I'll give that a proper try and see how it goes.
quests.correctAnswer: that is really helpful
acceptedSynonyms: that angle had not occurred to me

quests.hint: Use 'I'm a huge fan of…' to express a strong liking for something enthusiastically.
quests.explanation: 'I'm a huge fan of jazz' is far more expressive than 'I like jazz.' Using 'huge fan' shows genuine passion and enthusiasm, making you sound more natural and engaged in the conversation.
quests.situationText: Your new colleague is trying to find common ground and asks what kind of music you are into.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm a huge fan of jazz and soul music! Do you like live music? We should check out a gig together sometime - there are some great venues nearby.
quests.correctAnswer: jazz and soul music

quests.hint: Express a food preference: 'I tend to go for… when I'm given the choice between… and…'
quests.explanation: 'I tend to go for spicy food' uses 'tend to' which implies a consistent but not absolute preference. 'Go for' is a natural informal verb for choosing food - widely used by native speakers in everyday food chat.
quests.situationText: Someone asks whether you prefer spicy food or mild food, and asks you to explain your choice.
quests.sampleAnswer: I tend to go for spicy food every time - the more chilli, honestly, the better! I love the heat. Mild food just feels a bit bland to me now.
quests.correctAnswer: the spicier the better

quests.hint: Share a sporting passion: 'I'm absolutely passionate about… It keeps me sane, honestly.'
quests.explanation: 'I'm passionate about' is strong and positive for hobbies and activities you care deeply about. 'It keeps me sane' is a very natural, relatable English expression for an activity that relieves daily stress.
quests.situationText: A new friend asks what sport or physical activity you are most passionate about in your life.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm absolutely passionate about cycling. I try to get out at least four times a week - it genuinely keeps me sane and clears my head completely.
quests.correctAnswer: passionate about cycling

quests.hint: Use 'I'm not really a fan of…' to express dislike politely without sounding harsh or blunt.
quests.explanation: 'I'm not really a fan of horror films' is a gentle way to express dislike. It is much softer than 'I hate' and is far more comfortable in polite English conversation with people you are still getting to know.
quests.situationText: Your new friend suggests going to a horror movie and asks if that sounds good to you.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm honestly not really a fan of horror films - they give me nightmares! Would you be open to a thriller or a comedy instead?
quests.correctAnswer: not really a fan of horror films
acceptedSynonyms: not really a fan of horror films
open to a good thriller though

quests.hint: Use 'I'd rather… than…' to express a clear preference between two options.
quests.explanation: 'I'd rather walk than take the bus' uses the important grammatical structure 'would rather + base verb.' This expresses a definite preference between two alternatives and is widely used in everyday English.
quests.situationText: Your friend suggests taking the bus home but you feel like enjoying the evening by walking.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'd actually much rather walk tonight - it's such a lovely evening. It'll only take twenty minutes and I could use the fresh air.
quests.correctAnswer: much rather walk

quests.hint: Use 'I try to avoid…' to talk about things you consciously choose not to do or eat.
quests.explanation: 'I try to avoid' implies a deliberate, ongoing choice - stronger than 'I don't like' and implying self-discipline. This phrase works naturally when discussing dietary choices, habits, or lifestyle preferences.
quests.situationText: Someone offers you a large second portion of dessert and asks if you would like more.
quests.sampleAnswer: Thank you so much, but I try to avoid eating a lot of sugar in the evenings. I'll just have a herbal tea if there is one. Everything was delicious though!
quests.correctAnswer: trying to avoid eating too much sugar in the evenings
acceptedSynonyms: trying to avoid eating too much sugar in the evenings
